paper_metadata.title: High-temperature mechanical properties and radiation resistance properties of reduced-activation high-entropy alloys FeMnCrTi0.1

evidence.quote: This study investigates a previously developed BCC-phase RAHEA FeMnCrTi0.1 that demonstrates good mechanical properties at room temperature, exceeding those of current low-activation materials and most HEAs.

In this study, we investigated the high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance of the BCC phase reduced-activation high-entropy alloy FeMnCrTi0.1, which demonstrates good room-temperature mechanical performance.

The CLAM steel was provided by the Institute of Nuclear Energy Safety Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, and its specific composition and processing details can be found in reference [40].

The FeMnCrTi0.1 alloy was prepared using arc melting, with high-purity metal powders (purity > 99.5 %) sourced from Beijing Xingrongyuan New Materials Co., Ltd. Prior to melting, the chamber was repeatedly purged with high-purity argon gas, and a molten titanium ingot was employed to further adsorb oxygen. Each alloy ingot underwent five cycles of remelting, during which electromagnetic stirring was applied to enhance compositional homogeneity.

The high-temperature compression tests were conducted according to ASTM E9–09 standards using an electro-mechanical universal testing machines. Prior to compression, the samples were held at the test temperatures of 650℃, 800℃, and 950℃ for 30 minutes in air atmosphere, with the temperatures measured using thermocouples. The compression deformation rate was set at 10^3 s^1, and the experiments were terminated when the deformation reached 60 %

The implantation energy was set at 200 keV, with an ion beam current of 1 mA and a beam spot area of 0.785 cm2. The irradiation time was 55 minutes, with a corresponding hydrogen ion implantation flux of 2.59 × 1019 ions/cm2. According to the SRIM calculations, the maximum radiation damage level was estimated to be 100 displacements per atom (dpa).

Previous studies have shown that the FeMnCrTi0.1 alloy consists of two phases: BCC1 and BCC2, with a higher content of BCC2 compared to BCC1 [39]. These two BCC phases exhibit different deformation behaviors: BCC1 demonstrates ductility, while BCC2 shows hardness and brittleness.

Previous studies have shown that the FeMnCrTi0.1 alloy consists of two phases: BCC1 and BCC2, with a higher content of BCC2 compared to BCC1 [39]. These two BCC phases exhibit different deformation behaviors: BCC1 demonstrates ductility, while BCC2 shows hardness and brittleness.

In addition to the two BCC phases (BCC1 phase, space group Im-3m; BCC2 phase, space group I-43m) observed at room temperature, an HCP phase (space group P63/mmc) was detected in the selected area electron diffraction patterns.
Further analysis indicates that this phase is a Laves intermetallic compound [39].
